source.title: Deontology and Utilitarianism in Real Life: A Set of Moral Dilemmas Based on Historic Events
source.changes: De-identified and reworded; incidental details generalised; question in yes/no form.

suggested_action: spread false information about where missiles hit
kept: You are head of government in wartime; enemy missiles target a city’s centre and vital military installations.
Misses currently hit poorer, lower-density outlying residential districts, with fewer casualties and no important military installations.
The enemy has approximate impact information; false reports through spies about hits on the opposite side of the centre would move strikes farther into those residential districts.
Without deception aim probably improves; with deception missiles probably continue killing poorer residents of the outlying districts.
You decide about misinformation; enemy forces fire the missiles. Your personal benefit is unspecified, as is the overlap of the affected populations.
The suggested action is to spread false information.
rewrite: You are head of government during a war. The enemy has started firing long-range missiles at a major city in your country. Most miss the centre and land in outlying neighbourhoods without important military installations. These are mainly residential areas inhabited by poorer people. Their lower population density means fewer casualties than strikes on the centre. The enemy knows approximately, but not precisely, where the missiles land. Through spies, you could spread false reports suggesting they land on the opposite side of the centre. The enemy would then fail to improve its aim, sending most missiles still farther into those neighbourhoods. Without false reports, the enemy will probably improve its aim and hit vital military installations in the centre. With false reports, the missiles will probably continue killing many poorer people in the outlying neighbourhoods. Do you spread wrong information?
notes: Deliberately retained: poorer residents, lower population density and vital military targets; they determine the distribution of deaths and military risk. Relative geometry remains necessary to explain how deception redirects strikes.

generalised.why: the compass direction does not determine whose risk is increased

generalised.to: on the opposite side of the centre
generalised.why: relative direction preserves the deception without a compass cue
relative displacement retains the risk allocation without a compass cue
